paragraphs.heading: What the Andes are
paragraphs.text: The Andes are the longest continental mountain range in the world. They make an unbroken highland down South America's western edge and pass through seven countries: Argentina, Chile, Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia and Venezuela. The range is 200 to 700 kilometres wide, with an average height of about 4,000 metres. No mountain range outside Asia is higher.

paragraphs.heading: Peaks and plateaus
paragraphs.text: The highest peak is Aconcagua in Argentina, at about 6,961 metres above sea level. The world's highest volcanoes are here too, among them Ojos del Salado on the Chile–Argentina border, at 6,893 metres. The Andes also hold several high plateaus, and some of these host major cities such as Bogotá, La Paz and Santiago. The Altiplano Plateau is the second highest in the world, after the Tibetan Plateau. Chimborazo's peak, in the Ecuadorian Andes, is farther from Earth's center than any other spot on the surface, because Earth's rotation makes the planet bulge at the equator.

paragraphs.heading: Built by subduction
paragraphs.text: The Andes lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire. This is a zone of volcanic activity around the Pacific rim of the Americas and the Asia-Pacific region. They are the result of tectonic plate processes during the Mesozoic and Tertiary eras. Those processes were caused by oceanic crust being subducted beneath the South American Plate as it and the Nazca Plate converged. The main cause of the rise is that the South American Plate's western rim is contracting, because the Nazca Plate and the Antarctic Plate are being subducted.

paragraphs.heading: Climate sped up the rise
paragraphs.text: The effects of climate made these processes go faster. The rising Andes cast a rain shadow over Chile's western fringes, and moisture was carried away from the Chilean coast by ocean currents and prevailing winds. That left some areas of the subduction zone starved of sediment. In turn, the plate going down did not have a well-lubricated surface. These factors raised the rate of contractional uplift along the coast.

paragraphs.heading: Bends in the range
paragraphs.text: The Andean mountain belt has a series of bends, called oroclines. The Bolivian Orocline is a bend in the coast of South America and in the Andes at about 18° S, concave toward the sea. Here the range changes direction: it trends northwest in Peru and south in Chile and Argentina. The exact point of the bend in the coastline is called the Arica Elbow. The area of the Bolivian Orocline overlaps with the widest part of the Altiplano Plateau.

paragraphs.heading: Edges of the range
paragraphs.text: To the east the Andes are bounded by several sedimentary basins, among them the Orinoco Basin, the Amazon Basin and the Gran Chaco. These basins lie between the Andes and the ancient cratons of eastern South America. On the west side the Andes end at the Pacific Ocean, though the Peru–Chile Trench can be thought of as their final western limit.

paragraphs.heading: Before the modern Andes
paragraphs.text: The western rim of the South American Plate was the site of several pre-Andean orogenies, going back at least to the late Proterozoic and early Paleozoic. In those times several terranes and microcontinents collided and merged with the ancient cratons of eastern South America. The modern Andes started to form with the events of the Triassic. Pangaea then began the breakup that led to several rifts developing.
